opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to ask: human-like *for what*? "Human-like" isn't a goal in itself. It's useful only when it helps the agent do something valuable in an environment that was built for humans.

There are really two different senses of human-like. One is the **interface**. Our digital world, with its websites, software, documents, and workflows, was designed for human eyes and hands. If you want an agent to operate there, it often helps to perceive and act somewhat like a person: read a screen, click, type, follow instructions written in natural language. That kind of human-likeness is practical. It's about compatibility with the world we already have.

The other sense is the **internal way of working**: reasoning in language, thinking before acting, learning from experience, using memory. Here I'd say we should borrow from humans when it gives the agent real generalization ability, not just imitate for its own sake. Language-based reasoning is powerful because language is the most general tool humans invented for thinking. But there's no reason an agent has to stay within human limits. It can read much faster, run many trials in parallel, and keep far more context. Forcing it to be human-like there would be a waste.

So my rough rule is this. Be human-like where the environment or the collaboration demands it, and be non-human-like where the machine has a natural advantage.

There's also a third dimension people often overlook, which is **the relationship with the user**. If an agent works alongside people, it needs some human-like qualities: understanding intent, asking clarifying questions, knowing when to check in versus just get on with it, having some consistency over time. That's less about intelligence and more about being a good collaborator. I think this part will matter more and more. Over the next phase, the bottleneck isn't only whether the model can solve a hard problem. It's whether it can fit into real human workflows and create real value.

So I don't think of it as a single slider from "machine" to "human." It's a design question you answer differently for each layer, and the answer always comes back to utility. Does this make the agent more useful in the real world? If yes, make it more human-like there. If not, don't.

r001.rationale: The response says human-likeness is useful only when it helps the agent do something valuable, and recommends it where it improves usefulness in the real world.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the question itself is a bit of a trap, because "more human-like" is not actually the goal. It's a heuristic. The goal is for the agent to be useful, and humans happen to be the best example we have of a general-purpose agent, so we borrow from them. But we should borrow selectively.

When I was working on ReAct, the idea of interleaving reasoning and acting came from observing how people do tasks. You think a little, you do something, you see what happens, you think again. That turned out to be a very good inductive bias for language models. But notice we did not copy everything about humans. We did not give the model a limited working memory or make it tired after eight hours. We took the piece that was useful and left the rest.

So the way I think about it is: what is the bottleneck? If the agent fails because it cannot plan, or cannot recover from mistakes, or cannot use tools, then look at how humans handle those situations and ask whether that structure transfers. Human-likeness is a source of hypotheses, not a target. Tree of Thoughts came from the same place. People explore multiple possibilities and backtrack when something does not work, and that is a search procedure you can write down and test.

There is also a second reason to care about human-likeness, which is interface. If an agent operates in environments built for humans, like websites or software or documents, then being human-like in its actions is just practical. That was the whole motivation behind WebShop and later SWE-bench. The world is already designed around what a person can do, so an agent that can act like a person gets access to all of it for free.

But where I think people go wrong is treating human-likeness as an end in itself. A language model can read a thousand documents in parallel. It can run a hundred experiments at once. Forcing it to be sequential and bounded like a person would be throwing away the actual advantage. The interesting agents of the next few years will probably look human at the interface layer and very non-human in how they actually operate underneath.

So my honest answer is that I do not decide in the abstract. I look at a task, I look at where the model breaks, and I ask whether the way humans solve it gives me an idea. Sometimes yes, sometimes no. The environment and the evaluation tell you the answer much more reliably than any philosophy about what an agent should be.

r001.rationale: The response says human-likeness is useful when it helps with a task’s bottleneck, and that the environment and evaluation determine whether it works. This communicates that the choice depends on whether it improves task performance.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: which aspect of being human would actually help? “Human-like” is a very broad goal. If you mean understanding what someone wants, communicating clearly, or recognizing when to ask for clarification, those are useful qualities. But if you mean having all of our limitations and biases, there’s no obvious reason to reproduce those.

For an agent, I would start with the task and the person using it. Where does it need to adapt to human expectations so that collaboration works? And where could it do something differently and be more useful? You might want it to communicate in a familiar way, while being much more systematic than a person about checking its work.

So I wouldn’t treat becoming more human-like as the objective itself. I’d treat it as a design choice: does this particular human-like behavior make the agent more useful, easier to understand, and easier to correct?

r001.rationale: The response says to start with the task and treat human-like behavior as a design choice based on whether it helps the agent be more useful, communicating that human-likeness should depend on its value for task performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: which aspect of being human would actually help the agent? “Human-like” is a very broad goal. We might want an agent to understand our intentions, communicate clearly, and know when to ask for help. But we probably don’t want it to reproduce our biases, get distracted, or pretend to have feelings just to seem more relatable.

So I would start from the task and the interaction. If an agent is collaborating with you over a long period, remembering context and adapting to your communication style can be useful. If it’s executing a well-defined task, maybe you care much more about reliability and whether you can verify the result.

There’s also a distinction between having useful capabilities that humans have and presenting itself as a human. Those don’t have to go together. An agent can understand uncertainty or reason about someone’s perspective while still being transparent that it’s an AI.

For me, the test is whether making it more human-like helps people understand it, work with it, and maintain control. Human similarity itself isn’t the objective.

r001.rationale: The response says to start from the task and ask which human-like traits would help the agent, then gives examples of traits useful for collaboration versus well-defined tasks. This communicates that the decision depends on whether human-likeness helps with the task.
